## Learning Objectives

By the end of today, you will be able to:

- Explain why exploratory data analysis (EDA) is a critical 1st step before modeling EHR data
- Use **skimr** and other packages to profile a clinical dataset quickly
- Build publication-quality descriptive tables ("Table 1") with **gtsummary**
- Check univariate and multivariate distributions using appropriate diagnostics
- Create histograms, density plots, and comparison visuals with **ggplot2**
- Identify missingness, outliers, and data-quality issues unique to EHR data
- Recognize censoring in time-to-event EHR data and perform survival-specific EDA

---

## Why EDA Matters for EHR Data

EHR data is:

- **Observational, not experimental** — collected for clinical/billing purposes, not research
- **Messy** — missingness is informative (missing-not-at-random), duplicate encounters, unit inconsistencies
- **High-dimensional and mixed-type** — labs (continuous), diagnoses (categorical/coded), notes (text), time series (vitals)
- **Time-to-event in nature** — death, readmission, and disease onset are censored by follow-up windows, not fully observed

> Before you model anything, you must understand what you're modeling. EDA is where data errors are caught *before* they become "findings"

---

## A Typical EDA Workflow

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 9
flowchart LR
  A[Raw EHR extract] --> B[Structure check</br>dim, types, keys]
  B --> C[Missingness &<br>quality audit]
  C --> D[Univariate<br>distributions]
  D --> E[Descriptive tables<br>Table 1]
  E --> F[Bivariate / group<br>comparisons]
  F --> G[Time-to-event &<br>censoring checks]
  G --> H[Flag anomalies,<br>plan modeling]
```

## Setting Up: Packages for Today

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| eval: false

install.packages(c(
  "tidyverse",    # data wrangling + ggplot2
  "skimr",        # quick data summaries
  "gtsummary",    # publication-ready summary tables
  "gt",           # table rendering engine used by gtsummary
  "naniar",       # missing data visualization
  "visdat",       # visual data structure/type overview
  "dlookr",       # diagnose, describe, and visualize data
  "inspectdf",    # column-wise inspection & comparison
  "correlationfunnel", # correlation vs. binary outcome
  "ggstatsplot",  # stats-annotated ggplot visuals
  "patchwork",    # combine multiple ggplots
  "easystats",    # report, performance, see
  "survival",     # core survival analysis
  "survminer",    # Kaplan-Meier & diagnostic plots
  "ggsurvfit",    # modern tidy survival plotting
  "condsurv"      # conditional survival & censoring helpers
))
```

```{r}
#| label: library-load
library(tidyverse)
library(skimr)
library(gtsummary)
library(naniar)
library(visdat)
library(dlookr)
library(patchwork)
library(survival)
library(survminer)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 14))
```

---

## Simulating a Realistic (Synthetic) EHR Cohort

We simulate an inpatient/longitudinal cohort — no real patient data is used.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-data
set.seed(42)
n <- 1200

ehr <- tibble(
  patient_id   = sprintf("PT%05d", 1:n),
  age          = round(rnorm(n, mean = 62, sd = 16)),
  sex          = sample(c("Female", "Male"), n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.52, 0.48)),
  race_eth     = sample(c("White", "Black", "Hispanic", "Asian", "Other"),
                         n, replace = TRUE, prob = c(0.55, 0.18, 0.15, 0.08, 0.04)),
  bmi          = pmax(14, rnorm(n, mean = 29, sd = 6)),
  sbp          = round(110 + 0.35 * (age - 62) + rnorm(n, mean = 0, sd = 15)),
  ldl          = round(rnorm(n, mean = 110, sd = 35)),
  diabetes     = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-2 + 0.04 * (age - 60))),
  a1c          = round(ifelse(
    diabetes == 1,
    rgamma(n, shape = 6, scale = 1.3) + 5.5,   
    rnorm(n, mean = 5.4, sd = 0.3)              
  ), 1),
  hypertension = rbinom(n, 1, plogis(-1.5 + 0.05 * (age - 60))),
  los_days     = round(rgamma(n, shape = 1.6, scale = 2.4), 1),
  readmit_30d  = rbinom(n, 1, 0.12),
  admit_source = sample(c("ED", "Direct", "Transfer"), n, replace = TRUE,
                         prob = c(0.65, 0.25, 0.10))
)

# Inject realistic messiness: missingness + a few implausible values
ehr <- ehr |>
  mutate(
    bmi  = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.08, NA, bmi),
    ldl  = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.15, NA, ldl),
    a1c  = ifelse(runif(n) < 0.30, NA, a1c),  # not everyone gets an A1c
    sbp  = ifelse(row_number() %in% sample(1:n, 3), 999, sbp) # sentinel/error codes
  )

glimpse(ehr)
```

---

## Step 1: Structural Overview with `skimr`

```{r}
#| label: skim-overview
skim(ehr)
```

---

## Zooming In with `skimr`

```{r}
#| label: skim-subset
ehr |>
  select(age, bmi, sbp, ldl, a1c, los_days) |>
  skim() |>
  yank("numeric")
```

- Inline sparkline histograms flag skew (`los_days`) and impossible values (`sbp` max = 999) immediately
- `skim()` output is a tidy data frame — usable directly in later chunks

---

## Step 2: Auditing Missingness — `naniar`

```{r}
#| label: naniar-vis-miss
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
naniar::vis_miss(ehr, sort_miss = TRUE)
```

---

## Missingness Patterns and Co-occurrence

```{r}
#| label: naniar-upset
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
naniar::gg_miss_upset(ehr)
```

> `a1c` missingness is clinically meaningful: patients without diabetes
> risk factors (cholesterol) are less likely to have an A1c ordered

---

## Structure & Type Overview — `visdat`

```{r}
#| label: visdat
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
visdat::vis_dat(ehr)
```

---

## Cleaning Obvious Sentinel Errors

```{r}
#| label: clean-sentinels
ehr <- ehr |>
  mutate(
    sbp = na_if(sbp, 999),          # 999 was a data-entry sentinel
    age = ifelse(age < 0 | age > 105, NA, age)
  )

naniar::miss_var_summary(ehr) |>
  filter(n_miss > 0)
```

Always ask: *is this missing value random, a workflow artifact, or a coding error?*

Note: rewriting `ehr` for exercise, but in practice don't change your raw data!

---

## Step 3: Automated Diagnostics — `dlookr`

```{r}
#| label: dlookr-diagnose
dlookr::diagnose(ehr) |>
  arrange(desc(missing_percent))
```

```{r}
#| label: dlookr-numeric
dlookr::diagnose_numeric(ehr) |>
  select(variables, min, mean, median, max, outlier)
```

---

## Step 4: Descriptive Table 1 with `gtsummary` 

```{r}
#| label: gtsummary-table1
ehr |>
  select(age, sex, race_eth, bmi, sbp, ldl, a1c,
         diabetes, hypertension, los_days, admit_source) |>
  tbl_summary(
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{mean} ({sd})",
                     all_categorical() ~ "{n} ({p}%)"),
    missing = "ifany",
    missing_text = "Missing"
  ) |>
  bold_labels()
```

---

## Comparing Groups: Readmitted vs. Not

```{r}
#| label: gtsummary-compare
ehr |>
  mutate(readmit_30d = factor(readmit_30d, labels = c("No", "Yes"))) |>
  select(age, sex, bmi, sbp, ldl, a1c, diabetes,
         hypertension, los_days, readmit_30d) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = readmit_30d,
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})"),
    missing = "ifany"
  ) |>
  add_p(test = list(all_continuous() ~ "wilcox.test",
                    all_categorical() ~ "chisq.test")) |>
  add_overall() |>
  bold_labels() |>
  bold_p(t = 0.05)
```

What are problems/limitations with statistics presented here?

## Step 5: Checking Distributions — Histograms

```{r}
#| label: hist-basic
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(ehr, aes(x = los_days)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, fill = "#2C6E91", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Length of Stay Distribution",
       x = "Length of stay (days)", y = "Count")
```

Right-skewed — typical of LOS, cost, and count-type clinical variables.

---

## Multiple Distributions at Once

```{r}
#| label: hist-facets
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
ehr |>
  select(age, bmi, sbp, ldl, a1c, los_days) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "variable", values_to = "value") |>
  filter(!is.na(value)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#2C6E91", color = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ variable, scales = "free", ncol = 3) +
  labs(title = "Univariate Distributions of Key Clinical Variables",
       x = NULL, y = "Count")
```

  ggplot(aes(x = readmit_30d, y = los_days, fill = readmit_30d)) +

## Combining Panels with `patchwork`

```{r}
#| label: patchwork-combo
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 5.5
p1 <- ggplot(ehr, aes(age)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "#2C6E91", color = "white") +
  labs(title = "Age")

p2 <- ggplot(ehr, aes(x = sex, y = bmi, fill = sex)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white") +
  labs(title = "BMI by Sex", x = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

p1 + p2
```

## Stats-Annotated Visuals — `ggstatsplot`

Helpful when adding stats to `ggplot2` objects.

```{r}
#| label: ggstatsplot-demo
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
library(ggstatsplot)
ehr |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, labels = c("No", "Yes"))) |>
  ggbetweenstats(
    x = diabetes, y = a1c,
    title = "A1c by Diabetes Status",
    type = "nonparametric",
    xlab = "Diabetes diagnosis", ylab = "Hemoglobin A1c (%)"
  )
```

What if A1c high in people with "no" diabetes diagnosis?

## Correlation Structure — Numeric Variables

```{r}
#| label: corr-heatmap
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 5.5
ehr |>
  select(age, bmi, sbp, ldl, a1c, los_days) |>
  cor(use = "pairwise.complete.obs") |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  ggplot(aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile(color = "white") +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3.5) +
  scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#C1440E", mid = "white", high = "#2C6E91",
                        midpoint = 0, limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Pairwise Correlations", x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "r") +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

# Survival & Censoring EDA {background-color="#1B4332"}

## Why Time-to-Event Data Needs Its Own EDA 

Many EHR outcomes are **time-to-event**, not one-off measurements:

- Time to death, readmission, disease progression, device failure
- Follow-up ends before the event happens for many patients → **censoring**
- Standard histograms/means on "time" alone are **misleading** if you ignore censoring

**Types of censoring in EHR data:**

- **Right censoring** — follow-up ends (study end, loss to follow-up, transfer of care) before the event occurs
- **Left censoring** — event already happened before observation began (e.g., undiagnosed disease onset)
- **Interval censoring** — event known only to have occurred between two visits
- **Competing risks** — a different event (e.g., death from another cause) precludes the event of interest

---

## Simulating Time-to-Event Data with Censoring 

```{r}
#| label: simulate-survival
set.seed(42)

surv_df <- ehr |>
  mutate(
    true_event_time = rexp(n, rate = 0.002 * exp(0.015 * (age - 60) + 0.4 * diabetes)),
    admin_censor_time = 730,
    loss_fu_time = runif(n, min = 30, max = 730),
    time = pmin(true_event_time, admin_censor_time, loss_fu_time),
    status = case_when(
      true_event_time <= pmin(admin_censor_time, loss_fu_time) ~ 1L, # event observed
      TRUE ~ 0L                                                       # censored
    )
  ) |>
  select(patient_id, age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, time, status)

glimpse(surv_df)
```

---

## First Look: Censoring Rate & Follow-Up Time 

```{r}
#| label: censoring-summary
surv_df |>
  summarise(
    n              = n(),
    n_events       = sum(status == 1),
    n_censored     = sum(status == 0),
    pct_censored   = mean(status == 0) * 100,
    median_fu_days = median(time),
    max_fu_days    = max(time)
  )
```

```{r}
#| label: censoring-by-group
surv_df |>
  group_by(diabetes) |>
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    pct_censored = mean(status == 0) * 100,
    median_fu = median(time)
  )
```

> Always report the censoring proportion *before* fitting any survival model —
> a >50% censoring rate changes how much you should trust tail estimates.

---

## Visualizing Follow-Up Time and Event Status 

```{r}
#| label: followup-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
surv_df |>
  slice_sample(n = 60) |>
  arrange(time) |>
  mutate(id = row_number(),
         status_lab = factor(status, labels = c("Censored", "Event"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, y = id, color = status_lab)) +
  geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = time, y = id, yend = id), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Censored" = "#7a7a7a", "Event" = "#C1440E")) +
  labs(title = "Follow-Up Time per Patient (random sample of 60)",
       x = "Days since baseline", y = "Patient (sorted by follow-up time)",
       color = NULL) +
  theme(axis.text.y = element_blank(), axis.ticks.y = element_blank())
```

This "lollipop" or swimmer-style plot is a core EDA visual for time-to-event data —
it makes censoring visible at the individual level, not just as a summary statistic.

---

## Histogram of Observed Time, Stratified by Status

```{r}
#| label: time-hist-status
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
surv_df |>
  mutate(status_lab = factor(status, labels = c("Censored", "Event"))) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = time, fill = status_lab)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 40, alpha = 0.8, position = "identity") +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Censored" = "#7a7a7a", "Event" = "#C1440E")) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Observed Follow-Up Time",
       x = "Time (days)", y = "Count", fill = NULL)
```

---

## The Kaplan-Meier Estimator as an EDA Tool 

```{r}
#| label: km-overall
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
km_fit <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ 1, data = surv_df)

ggsurvplot(
  km_fit,
  data = surv_df,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  xlab = "Days since baseline",
  ylab = "Event-free probability",
  title = "Overall Kaplan-Meier Curve",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)
```

The **risk table** below the curve is itself an EDA device: it shows how many
patients remain under observation at each time point — a shrinking risk set
means later parts of the curve are estimated from very few patients.

---

## Comparing Survival Across Groups 

```{r}
#| label: km-by-diabetes
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
km_group <- survfit(Surv(time, status) ~ diabetes, data = surv_df)

ggsurvplot(
  km_group,
  data = surv_df,
  conf.int = TRUE,
  risk.table = TRUE,
  pval = TRUE,
  legend.labs = c("No Diabetes", "Diabetes"),
  xlab = "Days since baseline",
  ylab = "Event-free probability",
  title = "Kaplan-Meier by Diabetes Status",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)
```

The log-rank p-value here is descriptive/exploratory — it flags a group
difference worth investigating further, not a final causal conclusion.

---

## Checking the Proportional-Hazards Assumption Visually 

```{r}
#| label: cloglog-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggsurvplot(
  km_group,
  data = surv_df,
  fun = "cloglog",
  legend.labs = c("No Diabetes", "Diabetes"),
  xlab = "Days since baseline (log scale)",
  ylab = "log(-log(Survival))",
  title = "Complementary Log-Log Plot",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)
```

Roughly parallel curves on the cloglog scale support the proportional-hazards
assumption — a quick visual EDA check *before* committing to a Cox model.

---

## Cumulative Incidence / Hazard-Style View

```{r}
#| label: cumhaz-plot
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5.5
ggsurvplot(
  km_group,
  data = surv_df,
  fun = "cumhaz",
  conf.int = TRUE,
  legend.labs = c("No Diabetes", "Diabetes"),
  xlab = "Days since baseline",
  ylab = "Cumulative hazard",
  title = "Cumulative Hazard by Diabetes Status",
  ggtheme = theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
)
```

---

## Table 1 for Survival Cohorts — `gtsummary`

```{r}
#| label: gtsummary-survival
surv_df |>
  select(age, sex, diabetes, hypertension, time, status) |>
  mutate(status = factor(status, labels = c("Censored", "Event"))) |>
  tbl_summary(
    by = status,
    statistic = list(all_continuous() ~ "{median} ({p25}, {p75})")
  ) |>
  add_overall() |>
  bold_labels()
```

`gtsummary` also has `tbl_survfit()`, which reports survival probabilities
(e.g., 1-year, 2-year event-free rates) directly as a formatted table:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-survfit
tbl_survfit(
  km_group,
  times = c(180, 365, 730),
  label_header = "**{time} days**"
)
```

---

## Survival EDA Checklist 

1. **Quantify censoring** — overall % censored, and by key subgroups
2. **Distinguish censoring types** — administrative end-of-study vs. loss-to-follow-up vs. competing risk
3. **Visualize individual follow-up** — swimmer/lollipop plots to catch anomalies (e.g., negative or zero time)
4. **Plot Kaplan-Meier curves** with risk tables — don't trust the tail where the risk set is thin
5. **Check assumptions visually** — cloglog plots before assuming proportional hazards
6. **Compare groups descriptively** before any formal Cox modeling
7. **Watch for immortal time bias** — make sure time-zero is defined consistently across patients

---

## Putting It Together: A Full EDA Checklist for EHR Data 

1. **Structure** — dimensions, types, unique identifiers, duplicate rows/visits (`skimr`, `visdat`)
2. **Missingness** — patterns, mechanism (MCAR/MAR/MNAR), clinical plausibility (`naniar`)
3. **Data quality** — sentinel values, impossible ranges, unit mismatches (`dlookr`)
4. **Univariate** — shape, skew, outliers per variable (`ggplot2`, `skimr`)
5. **Descriptive tables** — stratified summaries with tests where appropriate (`gtsummary`)
6. **Bivariate/multivariate** — correlations, group comparisons (`ggstatsplot`)
7. **Time-to-event structure** — censoring rate, follow-up distribution, KM curves (`survival`, `survminer`)
8. **Document everything** — EDA decisions must be reproducible and justified

---

## Common EHR-Specific Pitfalls 

- **Informative missingness**: a missing lab often means "not clinically indicated," not "random"
- **Multiple encounters per patient**: don't treat visit-level rows as independent without checking
- **Left/right censoring**: patients enter/leave the system; "no diagnosis recorded" ≠ "no disease"
- **Immortal time bias**: exposure defined after time-zero can artificially inflate survival
- **Competing risks ignored**: treating death as censoring when it precludes the outcome of interest
- **Coding changes over time**: ICD-9 → ICD-10 transitions, billing code updates
- **Selection bias**: EHR cohorts reflect who sought/received care, not the general population

---

## Summary

- EDA is not a formality — for EHR data it is where most **real** data problems are found
- `skimr`, `visdat`, `naniar`, `dlookr` → fast structural and quality audits
- `gtsummary` → publication-ready descriptive, comparison, and survival tables
- `ggplot2` (+ `patchwork`, `ggstatsplot`) → distributions and visual group comparisons
- `survival` + `survminer` → Kaplan-Meier curves, risk tables, censoring diagnostics
- Always interpret findings **clinically**, not just statistically
